comparator.sourceNotes: The programme-specific 2026-2027 TER defines the 180-EC curriculum for ISAT 56003. The ordinary route represented here assumes the admitted student follows Greek and Latin Language Proficiency rather than a deficiency-transition module: year one is 60 EC, year two is 60 EC, and year three is a 30-EC minor plus 20 EC of Greek and Latin research seminars and a 10-EC thesis. The TER lists Greek and Latin transition modules for students without the relevant VWO final-examination preparation; these are conditional remediation and are not added to the 180-EC standard pathway. The faculty-wide course and minor remain explicit choice space rather than being filled with invented subjects.

exception.reason: The compulsory curriculum is organized around progressive proficiency and original-language reading in both Ancient Greek and Latin, followed by advanced Greek and Latin seminars, epigraphy and papyrology, original-language poetry analysis and a thesis in the field. UCR offers substantial adjacent work in archaeology, heritage, ancient history, philosophy, myth and comparative literature, but it offers neither Ancient Greek nor Latin language instruction and therefore no cumulative classical-philology sequence. A 24-course UCR programme assembled from those adjacent fields would omit the target's defining two-language core and would not be a defensible Classics match.
exception.curriculumContext: The official 2026-2027 TER accounts for exactly 180 EC in the standard non-deficiency pathway: 60 EC in year one, including 20 EC of Greek and Latin proficiency and 20 EC of first reading courses; 60 EC in year two, including 20 EC of second reading courses and specialist ancient-world research; and 60 EC in year three, consisting of a 30-EC minor, 10-EC Greek and Latin research seminars and a 10-EC thesis. Conditional Greek or Latin transition modules address missing pre-university preparation and are not extra degree credit in this reconstruction.
exception.ucrCourseEvidence: Reviewed all 151 current enriched UCR course rows, including descriptions, outline-derived profiles, topics, methods, prerequisites and planned terms. MCCHEAM112 Introduction to World Archaeology, MCCHEAM213 Greek Archaeology and MCCHEAM315 Heritage & Ancient Democracy provide strong ancient material-culture and heritage coverage; MCCLITR112 Great Literary Works and MCCLITR211 World Myth & Literature engage classical texts and reception; GOSHIST courses provide historical context; and GOSPHIL111 Introduction to Western Philosophy provides philosophical foundations. MCCCOMM211 Style & Meaning and HCBCOGN312 Psycholinguistics address language analytically, but no UCR course teaches Ancient Greek or Latin grammar, translation or original-language reading. None forms the prerequisite progression needed for Greek Reading 1 and 2, Latin Reading 1 and 2, epigraphy and papyrology, or advanced Greek and Latin research. The available ancient-world courses can support a coherent archaeology, heritage or reception programme, but they cannot reproduce the compulsory linguistic and philological core of this degree.
